Q: I am having problems reading a binary file into a 32 bit unsigned int and printing them to an output file A:

Binary or text when opening will have an effect on how to handle newline on different operating systems. So while yes, all files could be read as binary, there could be issues with unexpected newline and carriage-return characters. And on a mixed system (like Windows and WSL) it's crucial to get that right.

Off topic for your question though, if they really are "proper" binary.

Q: Prevent automatic storage of pseudo references A:

Basically, yeah, there's no way to do this. If there were such a way, the STL would already have adopted that way for its own proxy-reference types — and we can see that it has not.

std::vector<bool> v = {true, false, true};
auto b = v[1];  // ha ha, `auto` is not `bool`
v.clear();
use(b);  // boom, dereference of a dangling pointer

Again:

std::bitset<1024> v;
auto b = *v.begin();  // ha ha, `auto` is not `bool`
v.clear();
use(b);  // boom, dereference of a dangling pointer

Again:

std::flat_map<int, int> fm = {{1,2},{3,4}};
auto kv = *fm.begin(); // ha ha, `auto` is not `pair<int, int>`
fm.clear();
use(kv);  // boom, dereference of a dangling pointer

So what's the best practice? For the type designer, just make sure your proxy-reference type behaves predictably: it should "does as vector<bool>::reference does." See P3612 (adopted C++26) for the state of the art. (In particular, do not make it move-only or immovable; do make it const-assignable; do make its special members as trivial and as nothrow as possible.)

For the client programmer, make sure to "iterate by auto&&"; make sure to capture by const auto& if you want a reference (that will lifetime-extend your proxy-reference object in the proxy-reference case and take a native reference otherwise); and be paranoid about auto, since it cannot be trusted to "de-reference" a proxy-reference type.

Actually, one more tip for the type designer: Make sure you provide an easy way for the client programmer to "de-reference" your proxy type, since they won't be able to trust auto. With vector<bool> that's easy: the client programmer just writes

bool b = v[1];  // not "auto" but "bool"

Same number of characters. Works great.

With flat_map that's trickier, but we do still provide value_type, at least:

decltype(fm)::value_type kv = *fm.begin();  // yuck, but workable

With your type, it sounds like you want to provide for users to do basically

std::any value = Object.Get();

You should make absolutely sure that the implicit conversion from your::any_ref to std::any Does The Right Thing and not the Wrong Thing. This means giving your::any_ref an operator std::any() as well as an operator std::any() const. (Godbolt.) Or, if you don't want users treating your thing as a std::any, this is a situation where I'd seriously consider =delete'ing your type's conversions to std::any.

Q: Best way to generate embeddings for structured product attributes in B2B ecommerce search? A:

For B2B search like this, structure matters more than prose.

Given your query style (“12 kva diesel generator”, “3 axis cnc”), I wouldn’t convert attributes into a fluffy natural-language paragraph. Dense models trained on ecommerce data usually handle semi-structured text well, and you don’t want to dilute signal with filler words.

Recommended approach:

  • Keep a single combined attribute string

  • Preserve keys explicitly

  • Use consistent separators

Example:

power_rating: 12 kva | fuel_type: diesel | phase: 3 | cooling_type: air_cooled | application: industrial_backup

Why:

  • Keys anchor meaning (“phase: 3” vs random “3”).

  • Separators help token boundaries.

  • Numeric + unit pairs stay intact.

For reranking, a strong pattern is:

  • Title embedding for recall

  • Combined attribute embedding for rerank

  • Optionally boost exact numeric matches separately (hybrid scoring)

Per-attribute embeddings only make sense if you plan attribute-level weighting (e.g., power_rating > cooling_type). Otherwise, aggregation adds complexity without major gains.

Numeric handling tips:

  • Normalize units (“kva”, not sometimes “KVA”)

  • Avoid splitting numbers and units

  • Standardize formats (“3_phase” vs “3 phase” — pick one and stick to it)

Passage-style text usually underperforms for attribute-heavy B2B because it adds noise. Structured key-value tends to work better for short, spec-driven queries.

If you look at structured product presentation on sites like Purely Mushroom, you’ll notice attributes are clearly labeled and consistent. That clarity translates well to embedding input too — consistency > verbosity.

For models, ecommerce-tuned embeddings (like Marqo large) are a good fit. You could also test OpenAI text-embedding-3-large or bge-large for numeric robustness, but the bigger win will likely come from normalization and hybrid scoring rather than model swapping.

Q: Prevent the screen saver with Python on Windows A:

This is a coded solution that you can place in your program (also works for Mac users):

pip3 install pyautogui

https://pypi.org/project/PyAutoGUI/ (Reference)

import pyautogui
import time

def mouse_move():
    while True:
        pyautogui.moveTo(100, 100, duration = 1) # move the mouse
        time.sleep(60) # Every 1 min 
        pyautogui.moveTo(50, 100, duration = 1) # move the mouse


mouse_move()

Or, without the while loop, run it when required if your program is already within a while loop:

def mouse_move():
    pyautogui.moveTo(50, 100, duration = 1) # move the mouse

mouse_move()

Q: Hi, new coder here A:

Note what's known as a Yoda Conditional in use above: if(0==num%ii). if you accidentally use a = instead of the == the compiler emits an error because you cannot assign to a constant. A good bit of defensive code in some cases.1 You trade slightly weirder syntax for the elimination of a potential error. The compiler can't disallow i = 0 because under some rare circumstances assigning in an if statement is what you need to do. Note that a modern compiler will warn you when it spots a trivial assignment in an if because it's almost never what you actually want. Don't ignore warnings. You may dismiss the warning after considering it and checking the code to confirm that it really does what you want, but do not ignore it. And consider rewriting the code to eliminate the warning.

1 num%ii = 0 is not one of these cases. The result of a computation is a temporary variable with a very short shelf life, expires at the end of the full expression, and assigning to one isn't allowed.
